claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
The initial alloy has no detectable secondary phases.
High-strain-rate or low-temperature mechanical loading generates local stress concentrations.
Stress concentrations generated during severe loading drive local compositional fluctuations or segregation.
Stress-induced compositional segregation nucleates nanoscale precipitates or ordered domains.
The nanoscale precipitates or ordered domains are preferentially concentrated along grain boundaries.
The precipitates or ordered domains act as stress concentrators.
The precipitates disrupt uniform dislocation flow.
Disruption of dislocation flow promotes crack initiation.
The loading-induced microstructural changes lower ductility and toughness.
The loading-induced microstructural changes cause a transition toward brittle fracture.
Specimens subjected to high-strain-rate or low-temperature loading will have lower fracture toughness than specimens tested under moderate, room-temperature loading.
Specimens subjected to severe loading will exhibit more nanoscale segregation, precipitation, or ordered domains at grain boundaries than baseline specimens.
Under moderate, room-temperature loading, no significant phase segregation occurs.
Under moderate, room-temperature loading, no significant brittleness is observed.
Resistance to fracture decreases markedly beyond sufficiently high strain rates or sufficiently low operating temperatures.
Identical specimens should be compared under severe loading and moderate room-temperature loading while other processing conditions are held constant.
TEM and APT can be used to assess nanoscale precipitation and grain-boundary compositional segregation in the compared specimens.

The hypothesis is falsified if severe-loading specimens show no significant increase in nanoscale precipitation or grain-boundary segregation, or if their fracture toughness is not statistically lower than the baseline.
